notes.claim: Dividing by the base each time the exponent drops extends the pattern to zero and negative powers, and shows why a⁰ = 1.
Any base to the power of zero equals 1.
A negative power gives the reciprocal of the number, which is 1 over the number.
A common misconception is that a negative power makes the result negative, and it does not.
An older SQA Higher National unit, Introductory Mathematics for Engineering, asks for answers left with positive indices (added for i2's practice).

sources.title: Negative exponent intuition (video) | Khan Academy
sources.quote: Continue the pattern of decreasing exponents by dividing by 'a', and see how it extends to zero and negative powers. While we're at it, we'll see why a^0 =1.

sources.title: Negative and fractional indices - GCSE Maths Revision - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: Any base to the power of zero equals 1 and any base to the power of one is the base itself.

sources.title: Engineer cadets maths refresher — Solent University Warsash
sources.quote: So a negative power gives the reciprocal of the number — that is, 1 over the number.

sources.title: Engineer cadets maths refresher — Solent University Warsash
sources.quote: A common misconception is that since the power is negative, the result must be negative: as you can see, this is not so.
